newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African drug firms mull legal fight over reforms.
newsitem.headline: S.African drug firms mull legal fight over reforms.

text.p: South African drug firms may return to the court room for a second legal battle against health care reforms proposed by Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma, a leading industry figure said on Wednesday.

Last October Zuma backed down over plans to make prescribing generic drugs mandatory as Britain's SmithKline Beecham Plc took the issue to court. A consultation process was then launched to look at possible changes to the plans.
However, draft legislation put forward this week has changed little, drug makers say, and the legal battle between industry and government could resume.
Mirryena Deeb, chief executive of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association (PMA), said firms were thinking of action, but no decision had yet been made.
"That decision has not been taken yet, because it is still a draft document," she said.
Health Ministry spokesman Vincent Hlongwane said the new proposals were put together after more than 300 consultations from the public, the drugs firms and other interested parties.
He said the plans did guarantee a choice to patients between generic drugs or their brand name equivalents. Generics are cheaper versions of branded drugs that have gone off patent.
"We will legislate that patients should be given the choice," he said.
However, Deeb said drug makers were worried that the wording of the draft legislation still makes the substitution of generic drugs mandatory.
"A pharmacist shall...dispense a therapeutically equivalent medicine instead of the medicine prescribed...unless expressly forbidden by the patient to do so," the draft reads.
Deeb said the use of the word "shall" was too close to enforcing mandatory substitution of generic medicines.
"If it says 'shall' it is like substitution (of generics)," she said.

Deeb said there were also worries that the legislation's definition of "therapeutically equivalent" was too broad. The act defines it as drugs having the same therapeutic effect from the same pharmaceutically active ingredients and dosages.
But Deeb said that definition was loose enough to involve substituting one type of drug for another that is chemically different.

Another area of dispute that could crop up is any attack on the industry's right to promote its brand names. The global pharmaceuticals industry jealously guards its brands in the cut and thrust business of selling drugs.
The draft states: "No person shall sell any medicine to the State if that medicine contains the brand name in its label."

Deeb said any attacks on the industry's intellectual property rights would be certain to provoke a legal fight. "We will defend our intellectual property rights. If that is violated we will go to court," she said.
The previous dispute with Zuma prompted fears that international drug firms may start to pull out of a South African industry they see as hostile.

Then Knut Seifert, chief executive of German drug giant Boehringer Mannheim's South African unit, said the industry was at risk. "If an industry is not welcome in a country, then companies have to think about down-sizing of operations and moving into a more friendly environment," he said.
